title: Boss: the bad afternoon
summary: Undo the right way in five real situations, then build the undo tools yourself.

steps.title: The scene
body: It is 4 p.m. on a busy day and everything goes wrong at once: a `reset --hard` typed into the wrong terminal, a
half-finished feature in the way of a hotfix, and a feature that shipped in three commits and now has to go.
For each one, pick the undo that fits: **is it pushed?** and **is it committed?** are the two questions that decide.
First the rules as code, then two real repositories on your own machine.

steps.prompt: You pushed `Add audit log` to `main` this morning. It turns out to leak user emails into the logs. Teammates have pulled. What do you do?
options: `git revert <hash>`, push, and then fix forward on a branch
`git commit --amend` to remove the logging, then push
Ask everyone to delete their clones
steps.explain: Shared history only grows. Revert is the safe, auditable undo. (If the leak exposed data, also handle the incident: the logs themselves need cleaning.)

steps.prompt: Your branch `cart` was `A---B---C---D`. You typed `git reset --hard HEAD~3` by mistake, then made one new commit `E`. What does `git reflog` show for `HEAD@{2}`? Answer with the commit letter.
code: git reset --hard HEAD~3   # cart now at A
git commit -m "E"         # cart now at E (parent A)
git reflog                # HEAD@{0}: commit E, HEAD@{1}: reset, HEAD@{2}: ?
steps.explain: `HEAD@{0}` is E, `HEAD@{1}` is where the reset landed (A), and `HEAD@{2}` is before the reset: D. `git branch recovered HEAD@{2}` gets B, C and D back.

steps.title: Undo advisor
prompt: Write `Advise(bool committed, bool pushed, bool keepChanges)` returning the command a senior engineer would suggest to undo **the last change**:
`-` means the value does not matter.
starter: static string Advise(bool committed, bool pushed, bool keepChanges)
solution: static string Advise(bool committed, bool pushed, bool keepChanges)
return keepChanges ? "git reset --soft HEAD~1" : "git reset --hard HEAD~1";
hints: Pushed commits always get `revert`, whatever `keepChanges` says.
template: Dojo.Eq("uncommitted, keep", "git restore --staged .", Advise(false, false, true));
Dojo.Eq("uncommitted, discard", "git restore .", Advise(false, true, false));
Dojo.Eq("pushed, keep", "git revert HEAD", Advise(true, true, true));
Dojo.Eq("pushed, discard", "git revert HEAD", Advise(true, true, false));
Dojo.Eq("local, keep", "git reset --soft HEAD~1", Advise(true, false, true));
Dojo.Eq("local, discard", "git reset --hard HEAD~1", Advise(true, false, false));

steps.title: Reset, then rescue
prompt: 4:05 p.m. in `~/payments`: someone typed `git reset --hard HEAD~2` in your terminal. Two commits are gone, and your
half-finished report work in `src/report.py` is in the way of an urgent hotfix.
1. Get `main` back to where it was before the reset, keeping the report work.

2. Hotfix: on a new branch `hotfix/rounding` started from that restored `main`, make `refund_total` in `src/money.py` round to cents, `round(sum(items), 2)`, and commit it as `Fix refund rounding`. Only `src/money.py` goes into that commit.
3. End on `main`, with the report work back in the working tree, uncommitted, and an empty stash.

checks.name: main is back where it was before the reset
checks.fail: `main` is not back at `Validate refund amount` yet. Read `git reflog`.

checks.name: hotfix/rounding is one commit on top of main
checks.cmd: cd ~/payments && test "$(git rev-parse -q --verify 'hotfix/rounding~1')" = "$(git rev-parse main)" && test "$(git log -1 --format=%s hotfix/rounding)" = "Fix refund rounding"
checks.fail: There is no branch `hotfix/rounding` with one `Fix refund rounding` commit on top of the restored `main`.

checks.name: the hotfix rounds to cents
checks.fail: The hotfix commit does not contain `round(sum(items), 2)`. `sed -i 's/old/new/' file` edits a line in place.

checks.name: the hotfix holds only src/money.py
checks.cmd: cd ~/payments && test "$(git diff --name-only main hotfix/rounding)" = src/money.py
checks.fail: The hotfix commit changes other files too. Park the report work before you commit.

checks.name: you are on main with the report work back
checks.cmd: cd ~/payments && test "$(git branch --show-current)" = main && grep -q 'group by day' src/report.py && test -z "$(git stash list)"
checks.fail: Finish on `main` with the report work in `src/report.py` and an empty `git stash list`.

checks.name: the report work is not committed anywhere
checks.cmd: cd ~/payments && ! git log --all -p -- src/report.py | grep -q 'group by day'
checks.fail: The half-finished report work ended up in a commit. It should stay uncommitted.

hints: Order matters: park the report work (`git stash push`) before any command that resets the working tree.
`git reflog` shows where `main` was before the reset; pin it with a branch, or use `git reset --hard HEAD@{1}` before HEAD moves again.
Hotfix: `git switch -c hotfix/rounding`, `sed -i 's/round(sum(items))/round(sum(items), 2)/' src/money.py`, `git commit -am "Fix refund rounding"`. Then `git switch main` and `git stash pop`.
steps.explain: Reflog for the committed work, stash for the uncommitted work, a branch for the hotfix: three tools, each for the one job it is safe at. (`git reset --keep HEAD@{1}` is a shortcut seniors like: it moves the branch but refuses to touch files you have edited.)

steps.title: Revert a whole series
prompt: In `~/site` everything is pushed. Product has decided dark mode must go. It came in three commits: `Add dark mode`,
`Dark mode toggle in header` and `Polish dark colours`. Since then Sam renamed Shop to Store in the header, and that stays.
- Revert all three, **newest first**, one revert commit each, with Git's default messages.
- One revert will **conflict**. Resolve it so the header keeps Sam's Store link and has no dark-mode button.
The terminal is line based, so edit with commands: `git checkout --ours <file>` takes your side of a conflict, and `sed -i '/pattern/d' <file>` deletes matching lines.

checks.name: three revert commits, newest first
checks.cmd: cd ~/site && test "$(git log -3 --format=%s | tr '\n' '|')" = 'Revert "Add dark mode"|Revert "Dark mode toggle in header"|Revert "Polish dark colours"|'
checks.fail: The last three commits should be the reverts, newest dark-mode commit reverted first: `git log --oneline -4` shows what you have.

checks.name: pushed history is untouched
checks.fail: Pushed commits were rewritten. Press Reset scenario: revert only adds commits.

checks.name: no dark mode left anywhere
checks.cmd: cd ~/site && ! grep -qi dark theme.css settings.js header.html

checks.name: the header keeps the Store link (and Home)
checks.fail: Sam's `Store` link (or the Home link) is missing from `header.html`.

checks.name: no conflict left, nothing in progress
checks.cmd: cd ~/site && ! grep -qE "^(<<<<<<<|=======|>>>>>>>)" header.html && ! test -e .git/REVERT_HEAD && ! test -d .git/sequencer && test -z "$(git status --porcelain)"
checks.fail: A conflict marker or an unfinished revert is still there. After fixing the file: `git add header.html` and `git revert --continue`.

hints: Newest first: `git revert --no-edit ':/^Polish dark colours'` (Git finds a commit by its message), then the toggle, then `Add dark mode`.

When the toggle revert stops with a conflict, `git diff` shows both sides. `git checkout --ours header.html` keeps the current header (with Store), and `sed -i '/dark-toggle/d' header.html` removes the button.
Then `git add header.html` and `git revert --continue`, which keeps Git's message.
solution: git revert --no-edit ':/^Dark mode toggle in header'
steps.explain: Reverting newest first means each revert applies to the code it was written against, so fewer conflicts. When one does conflict, it is an ordinary merge conflict: pick the right content, `git add`, continue. (`git revert --no-edit A B C` or a range `git revert OLD..NEW` does the whole series in one command.)
